::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Multiplying matrix by row of zeros results in zeros in column](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2662725/multiplying-matrix-by-row-of-zeros-results-in-zeros-in-column), asked by [user12888](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/526266/user12888) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2018-02-23; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> If I have a matrix $A$ which is $n\times n$ and I have another matrix $I$ which is almost the identity matrix but has some zeros in it’s diagonal entries, then the rows of zeros in $I$ make the columns of $A$ zeros. 
>
> For a concrete example see these two WA links:
> [Link 1][q-1]
> [Link 2][q-2]
>
> Why is this true (proof perhaps)? I'm not really sure how to word my Question since I don't really now what is happening.
>
>
>   [q-1]: http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=%7B%7B1,2%7D,%7B4,5%7D,%7B7,8%7D%7D%7B%7B1,2%7D,%7B4,5%7D,%7B7,8%7D%7D%5ET
>   [q-2]: http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=%7B%7B1,2,3%7D,%7B4,5,6%7D,%7B7,8,9%7D%7D*%7B%7B1,0,0%7D,%7B0,1,0%7D,%7B0,0,0%7D%7D*%7B%7B1,2,3%7D,%7B4,5,6%7D,%7B7,8,9%7D%7D%5ET
:::

When you multiply matrices $A$ and $B$, the $i$th column of the product is $A$ times the $i$th column vector of $B$.  

If that column is a “standard basis vector” $\vec{e}_j$, that is, a vector with all zeros except for one $1$ in the $j$th position, the result is the $j$th column of $A$.  

This means that if $B$ is a diagonal matrix, $AB$ is the same as $A$ after scaling each column by diagonal entry in the corresponding column of $B$:
$$\begin{bmatrix} \vec{a}_1 & \vec{a}_2 & \cdots & \vec{a}_n\end{bmatrix}
    \begin{bmatrix} \lambda _1 \\ & \lambda _2 \\ && \ddots \\ &&&\lambda_n \end{bmatrix}
   =\begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1\vec{a}_1 & \lambda_2\vec{a}_2 & \cdots & \lambda_n\vec{a}_n\end{bmatrix}$$
So if one of those $\lambda_i$'s is zero, the product $\lambda_i\vec{a}_i$ is the zero vector.
